body:
What Wi-Fi actually provides

Wi-Fi is a family of wireless local-area-network technologies based on IEEE 802.11 standards. It allows compatible devices to communicate over a relatively local radio network without using a cable for each device.

A Wi-Fi access point provides wireless connectivity to devices such as phones, computers and tablets. A home router commonly combines Wi-Fi access-point functions with the functions needed to connect the home network to an internet service provider.

Wi-Fi commonly uses the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands. Some newer Wi-Fi systems also support 6 GHz, where national rules permit it. Band availability and permitted operating conditions are matters of national regulation.

Wi-Fi is not itself the internet. A phone may be connected to a local Wi-Fi network even when that network has lost its broadband connection. Conversely, a phone can reach the internet through a cellular mobile network without using Wi-Fi.

Wi-Fi and cellular networks are different

FeatureWi-FiCellular network
Main standard familyIEEE 802.11Cellular standards including GSM, LTE and 5G NR
Typical service areaHome, office, institution or hotspotCells forming a wider operator network
Radio connectionDevice to Wi-Fi access pointDevice to cellular base station
Common purposeLocal wireless networkingWide-area mobile connectivity

Both technologies use radio waves for the local wireless connection. Both can also depend on optical-fibre links deeper in the network. A phone may switch between Wi-Fi and mobile data, but that does not make the 2 radio-access technologies identical.

Coverage, capacity, speed and latency

Coverage means where a usable connection is available. Capacity describes how much traffic a network can carry. Throughput is the amount of useful data actually transferred in a period, while latency is delay.

A Wi-Fi signal may be strong while internet performance is poor because the broadband connection is congested. A cellular phone may display an advanced network generation but receive limited speed because many users share the available resources. These observations show why a radio signal indicator alone cannot establish end-to-end internet performance.

Why building a telecommunications network is expensive

Network economics explains how infrastructure costs, scarce radio resources and user demand affect the provision of communication services. Telecommunications generally involves substantial fixed costs: acquiring sites, installing towers, laying fibre, purchasing equipment, obtaining necessary spectrum rights and maintaining power and connectivity.

Once infrastructure exists, carrying some additional traffic may cost less than constructing an entirely new route or tower. This can create economies of scale: when more subscribers use the same suitable infrastructure, its fixed costs can be spread across more users. However, capacity is not unlimited; expansion is needed when demand exceeds what the network can efficiently carry.

Backbone, backhaul and last mile

  • Backbone: high-capacity routes joining major parts of a communication network, such as cities and important network centres.
  • Backhaul: links connecting access networks or radio sites to the wider network.
  • Last mile: the final connection that reaches a home, shop, school or other customer premises.

The last mile may be provided by fibre to the premises, a local wireless link, cable or another suitable technology. A high-capacity backbone does not automatically mean every household has an active broadband subscription.

Why spectrum and network effects matter

Usable radio spectrum is scarce because incompatible transmissions can interfere with one another. Assigning and coordinating spectrum helps operators plan services. Licensed spectrum can therefore have substantial economic value.

Communication networks may also show network effects: a service can become more useful when more people and institutions can communicate through it. This is distinct from economies of scale, which concerns costs per user. More users may increase a network's value while simultaneously creating congestion if capacity is insufficient.

Rural and urban connectivity have different cost conditions

Dense urban areas may support more subscribers per network site, but buildings, interference and heavy traffic can make coverage complicated. Rural areas may require long fibre routes or radio coverage over large distances while serving fewer paying users. Public infrastructure programmes can help address areas where the commercial return alone may not justify investment.

Prelims focus

  • Wi-Fi belongs to the IEEE 802.11 wireless LAN family.
  • Wi-Fi commonly uses 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz radio bands.
  • A Wi-Fi connection does not necessarily mean the internet is available.
  • Backhaul connects an access network to the wider telecommunications network.
  • Economies of scale concern costs; network effects concern increasing usefulness as participation grows.
  • Trap: Strong signal, high bandwidth and low latency do not mean exactly the same thing.

[Sources: IEEE Standards Association, 'IEEE 802.11-2024', wireless LAN standard description, published 28 April 2025, consulted 4 November 2026; ITU Radiocommunication Bureau, 'Frequently Asked Questions', entries I002–I006 on spectrum management, consulted 4 November 2026; NCERT, Our Environment, Class 7, ch. 7, 'Human Environment — Settlement, Transport and Communication', printed pp. 52–53, 2018–19 edition; Department of Telecommunications, Digital Bharat Nidhi, Amended BharatNet Programme overview, consulted 4 November 2026.]

title: Wi-Fi, Mobile Internet and the Economics of Communication Networks

body:
Why public broadband infrastructure matters

Digital services require both computing facilities and reliable communication networks. Schools, health centres, Gram Panchayats, businesses and households need connectivity to exchange information and use online services. In places where network construction is commercially difficult, public programmes may support the creation and use of broadband infrastructure.

India's BharatNet programme is intended to expand high-speed broadband connectivity to Gram Panchayats and rural areas. Optical fibre forms an important part of the network, while different technologies may be used to reach individual consumers.

BharatNet: connecting Gram Panchayats

BharatNet provides network infrastructure towards the Gram Panchayat level so that internet services can be extended locally. The distinction between reaching a Gram Panchayat and connecting individual customers is essential.

A middle-mile network brings network capacity towards a local area, such as a Gram Panchayat. A last-mile connection then extends usable service to a household, institution or business. Last-mile provision may use fibre to the home (FTTH), public Wi-Fi or another suitable access technology.

The Union Cabinet approved the Amended BharatNet Programme on 4 August 2023. It provides for improvement and expansion of the network, including the use of ring networks that provide alternative paths if a link fails and greater emphasis on actual broadband utilisation. The programme's intended expansion is not equivalent to declaring every proposed connection completed.

Gujarat Fibre Grid Network Limited

Gujarat Fibre Grid Network Limited (GFGNL) is a Government of Gujarat special-purpose vehicle established on 30 September 2016 to implement BharatNet Phase II in Gujarat. It operates under the state government's Department of Science and Technology.

GFGNL's fibre network supports the objective of taking high-capacity connectivity towards Gram Panchayats and other locations. The network can support subsequent connections for public institutions, households and service providers.

Official Gujarat network status

According to the Gujarat Department of Science and Technology's published status as on 30 June 2026, GFGNL reported 41,059 km of optical-fibre cable laid and 8,019 Gram Panchayats lit. These are reported infrastructure-status figures for that date; they are not a count of household broadband subscribers or a claim about conditions on every later date.

A lit Gram Panchayat is a network-connectivity status. It should not be interpreted automatically as meaning every home in that Gram Panchayat has an installed and functioning internet connection.

PM-WANI: a framework for public Wi-Fi

PM-WANI stands for Prime Minister Wi-Fi Access Network Interface. It is an Indian framework designed to facilitate public Wi-Fi access through participating service providers and local hotspot operators.

Its principal roles include:

  • Public Data Office (PDO): operates a WANI-enabled public Wi-Fi access point or hotspot.
  • Public Data Office Aggregator (PDOA): aggregates PDO access points and handles functions such as authorisation, accounting and tariff-related arrangements.
  • App Provider: helps users discover participating hotspots and use the relevant access and authentication arrangements.
  • Central Registry: supports the registration and discovery framework for participating entities.

The Department of Telecommunications' public guidance distinguishes local PDO operation from the registration requirements applicable to aggregators and app providers. A PDO is not required to obtain a separate individual telecommunications authorisation merely to act as a PDO under the applicable framework. This does not remove other applicable operating conditions.

Public Wi-Fi is not necessarily free Wi-Fi. A participating service may charge users according to the applicable plan or tariff.

How BharatNet and PM-WANI can complement one another

BharatNet can provide network capacity towards a rural area, while a PM-WANI hotspot can provide a convenient local wireless access point. For example, a Gram Panchayat may have a broadband network connection, and a nearby participating shop may provide public Wi-Fi using a suitable backhaul service.

The programmes therefore address different parts of a connectivity problem: BharatNet primarily concerns broadband infrastructure and its utilisation, whereas PM-WANI concerns a framework for public Wi-Fi access. Neither programme is a cloud-computing service model.

Prelims focus

  • BharatNet aims to expand high-speed broadband connectivity to Gram Panchayats and rural areas.
  • The Amended BharatNet Programme was approved on 4 August 2023.
  • GFGNL was established on 30 September 2016 for BharatNet Phase II implementation in Gujarat.
  • GFGNL reported 41,059 km of fibre laid and 8,019 Gram Panchayats lit as on 30 June 2026.
  • PM-WANI roles include PDO, PDOA, App Provider and Central Registry.
  • Trap: A Gram Panchayat being connected or lit does not establish that every household has internet access; a PM-WANI hotspot need not be free.

[Sources: Department of Telecommunications, Digital Bharat Nidhi, 'Amended BharatNet Program', approval and implementation overview, consulted 4 November 2026; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Communications, 'Internet Connectivity in Rural and Remote Areas', 29 January 2026; Department of Science and Technology, Government of Gujarat, 'Gujarat Fibre Grid Network Limited', establishment details and status as on 30 June 2026, consulted 4 November 2026; Department of Telecommunications eServices Portal, 'PM-WANI / Public Data Office Aggregator', frequently asked questions, last updated 18 August 2026, consulted 4 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Gram Panchayat connectivity and household connectivity are separate stages of broadband delivery.

title: India and Gujarat: BharatNet, Public Wi-Fi and Digital Connectivity

body:
What is cloud computing?

Cloud computing is a way of obtaining computing resources such as processing power, storage, software and network services when they are needed through a network. Instead of owning and managing all the required equipment locally, an organisation can use computing resources provided and managed through a cloud infrastructure.

The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) describes cloud computing as a model that provides convenient, on-demand access to a shared pool of configurable computing resources that can be rapidly supplied and released with relatively little management effort.

The word cloud does not mean that information is stored in the atmosphere. Real cloud services depend on physical computers, storage devices, networking equipment, electricity, software and data centres. What changes is the way these resources are organised, accessed and managed.

How a cloud service works in everyday life

Consider an online examination-registration website. During an ordinary day, a moderate number of applicants may use it. Near the application deadline, many more applicants may try to access the website. A suitable cloud arrangement can provide additional computing resources to handle increased demand and later reduce those resources when traffic falls.

The user generally sees the website, not the individual physical server providing each response. Behind the service, cloud software coordinates the necessary computing and storage resources.

The 5 essential characteristics of cloud computing

NIST identifies 5 essential characteristics. Understanding each characteristic is more useful than memorising the list without its meaning.

  1. On-demand self-service: a consumer can obtain computing resources when needed through an automated process rather than waiting for a provider's employee to set up each individual request.
  2. Broad network access: cloud capabilities are accessible over a network through standard mechanisms suited to different devices, including computers, tablets and phones.
  3. Resource pooling: a provider combines computing resources to serve multiple consumers. Individual users are given suitable portions of the shared resources while their data and activities must remain appropriately isolated.
  4. Rapid elasticity: available computing capacity can be increased or reduced quickly according to demand. For the consumer, resources may appear readily expandable, although physical and contractual limits still exist.
  5. Measured service: resource use can be monitored and measured, such as by storage consumed, computing time or service usage. Measurement supports administration, accountability and charging.

What makes cloud computing different from ordinary internet access?

The internet is a global system of interconnected networks that carries information. Cloud computing is a model for providing computing resources and services over networks. The internet can be used to reach cloud services, but the 2 terms are not interchangeable.

Not every website or remote computer automatically satisfies the cloud-computing model. The defining characteristics include on-demand provisioning, pooled resources, elasticity and measured use. A private cloud may also operate through a restricted organisational network rather than being openly accessible through the public internet.

Benefits and limitations

Cloud computing can reduce the need to purchase enough equipment for the highest possible demand, support faster deployment of services and make resources accessible from different locations. It can also help organisations use shared infrastructure efficiently.

Cloud services nevertheless require careful management of data security, access rights, service costs and availability. Charges may increase as resource consumption grows. A service can be interrupted by network failure, provider disruption or faulty application configuration.

Measured service does not mean that a cloud service is free. It means usage can be measured. Similarly, rapid elasticity does not guarantee unlimited capacity under every circumstance.

The connection between telecommunications and cloud computing

Telecommunication networks carry data between users and cloud facilities. Cloud services process, store or deliver that data. A fast cloud computer cannot compensate fully for a failed internet connection, and an excellent broadband connection cannot repair a failed application server. The 2 systems complement one another but solve different problems.

Prelims focus

  • NIST SP 800-145, published in 2011, defines the widely used cloud-computing model.
  • Its 5 essential characteristics are on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity and measured service.
  • Cloud computing uses physical infrastructure; it is not computing without servers.
  • Elasticity concerns increasing and decreasing resources according to demand.
  • Measured service concerns recording and managing resource usage.
  • Trap: Cloud computing is not another name for the internet, and measured usage does not automatically mean zero cost.

[Sources: National Institute of Standards and Technology, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing, Special Publication 800-145, September 2011, sec. 2, printed p. 2, consulted 4 November 2026; NIST, 'Cloud Computing' project overview, updated 14 September 2026, consulted 4 November 2026; National Informatics Centre, 'National Cloud', service overview, consulted 4 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Users access an examination website through a network; its allocation from shared servers and storage can grow at the deadline and shrink as demand falls.
pictures.caption: Cloud infrastructure pools computing resources and can adjust their allocation as demand changes.

title: Cloud Computing: Meaning, Resources and Five Essential Characteristics
